nodes.title: Steel Reimagined
nodes.summary: Tata Steel UK is transforming its Port Talbot plant in Southern Wales by replacing coal-fueled blast furnaces, with the last decommissioned on September 30, 2024, with a state-of-the-art electric arc furnace (EAF) to produce low-emission steel. Approved in early 2025 and breaking ground this summer, the EAF is expected to be fully operational by 2027, producing 3.2 million tonnes annually and reducing on-site carbon emissions by up to 90% using recycled scrap. This positions Port Talbot at the forefront of sustainable steelmaking in Europe, shifting from virgin raw materials to a circular economy. The text also lists leadership sections: Board of Directors, Senior Management, Chairman's Message, and Management Speak, along with report details for the 118th year, Integrated Report & Annual Accounts 2024-25, pages 20-21.

nodes.title: Ensuring business resilience
nodes.summary: This text covers Tata Steel's business resilience strategy, detailing financial, macroeconomic, regulatory, commodity, supply chain, operational, safety, community, and cyber risks, along with mitigation measures. It discusses financial risk from expansion and low-emission transition, net debt, and sensitivity to global factors; mitigation via cash flow, portfolio restructuring, and ESG collaboration. Macroeconomic risks include global challenges, China oversupply, and European competitiveness, mitigated by product leadership and localisation. Regulatory risks involve CBAM and tariffs, mitigated by compliance and advocacy. Commodity risks from price volatility and supply dependency are managed through hedging and diversification. Supply chain risks from logistics and infrastructure are mitigated by partnerships and private freight. Operational risks from equipment failures and cyber threats are addressed via predictive maintenance and security measures. Safety and community risks are mitigated through policies and community programs. Cyber risks from technology adoption are managed with robust security frameworks.

nodes.title: Ethics and Compliance
nodes.summary:
Ethics and Compliance
Tata Steel fosters a culture of integrity and transparency, upholding legal compliance and ethical governance to build enduring stakeholder trust and ensure responsible, sustainable operations across its global footprint.

nodes.title: Guided by the Tata Code of Conduct
nodes.summary: Tata Steel's ethics approach follows the Tata Code of Conduct and the Management of Business Ethics (MBE) framework, built on leadership, compliance structure, communication and training, and measurement. Leadership involves Board and Management committees, the Chief Ethics Counsellor, Divisional Ethics Coordinators, Ethics Champions, and POSH representatives. Compliance uses IT systems like Darpan, MBE Information System, Kashmakash, Integrated Concern Management System, and a third-party 'Speak Up' helpline. Communication and training cover round-tables, vendor meetings, town halls, and tailored programmes on POSH, Tata Code of Conduct, respectful workplace, conflict of interest, anti-bribery, and third-party due diligence. Measurement includes an annual MBE Survey and in-person discussions. Human rights are overseen by the Apex Business & Human Rights Committee, with a policy aligned to global principles and the Tata Code, grievance mechanisms, value chain compliance with SA8000:2014, and no reports of modern slavery or human trafficking in FY2024-25. Compliance serves as a second line of defence, underwent an ISO 9001:2015 surveillance audit, aims for ISO 37301:2021 certification, integrates technology, and plans to extend oversight to third-party relationships. Data privacy covers collection, storage, retention, and transfer of personal data, robust security, limited collection on a need-to-know basis, and workshops, campaigns, training, and digital resources for stakeholders.

nodes.summary: This text details Tata Steel's relationship capital across stakeholder groups: investors and lenders (strategic capital, communication, ESG disclosures), customers (product mix, digital platforms like COMPASS, DigECA, Aashiyana, NPS 77), vendor partners (sustainability, governance, MSME support), government and regulatory bodies (policy advocacy, green steel plans in Netherlands/UK), employees (communication, safety, DE&I, EAF transition), communities (CSR, resettlement, youth support), media (proactive engagement), industry bodies (CII, FICCI, worldsteel), and academic institutions (research partnerships). It also covers raw material management, including iron ore and coal mining, production figures (40.5 MT iron ore), beneficiation plants, and by-product utilization.

nodes.title: T U R A L C A P I T
nodes.summary: Tata Steel's Integrated Report highlights its Net Zero by 2045 commitment, focusing on circularity, conservation, and innovation. It details raw material sourcing: 100% iron ore from captive mines in India (40.5 MT) and Canada (3 MT), clean coal from West Bokaro and Jharia, and manganese/chromite mines with ferroalloy plants. Water management includes reduction, recycling, and reuse initiatives across sites. Air pollution control features advanced technologies, real-time monitoring, and significant stack dust emission reductions. Solid waste management achieves 100% utilization at several sites, with value-added by-products like Tata Aggreto. Biodiversity management plans cover 27 sites, with recognition at Shotton. Scrap usage increases via EAF routes in the UK, Netherlands, Thailand, and India. The report also covers environmental policy, ISO 14001 certification, and climate change challenges.

nodes.title: Inclusive engagement for a sustainable future
nodes.summary: The section covers Tata Steel's inclusive engagement for a sustainable future, detailing governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics. Governance addresses global steel challenges and Tata Steel's decarbonisation efforts, including EAF facilities, biochar, responsible mining, water recycling, TNFD adoption, and governance structures like Board Committees and Centres of Excellence. Strategy outlines region-specific climate and nature plans: India's low-emission steelmaking, Carbon Bank, and decarbonisation roadmap to 2045; the UK's EAF facility; and the Netherlands' Groen Staal Plan. Risk management integrates climate and nature risks via ERM, TCFD-aligned assessments, community projects, and opportunities like green steel and carbon credits. Metrics cover ESG disclosures aligned with BRSR, GHG Protocol, and IFRS S2, including environmental metrics and targets in the Integrated Report.

nodes.title: A Governance
nodes.summary: The text covers global steel industry challenges (excess capacity, declining demand, rising costs) and solutions including fiscal support, clean energy policies, carbon pricing, and Nature-based Solutions. It details Tata Steel's decarbonisation efforts: a 3.2 MTPA EAF in the UK by 2027 to cut 50 million tonnes of CO2, EAF facilities in Thailand, a planned scrap-based plant in Ludhiana, biochar usage, responsible mining, water recycling, and collaboration with the Dutch Government. It discusses TNFD adoption integrated with TCFD (now IFRS S2), climate-risk assessments, and nature-related dependency analysis. Governance structure includes Board Committees, Apex Committees, Centres of Excellence for GHG and Biodiversity, and the TOP programme.

nodes.title: B Strategy
nodes.summary: Tata Steel's climate and nature strategy varies by geography. In India, it adopts low-emission steelmaking, plans renewable energy increases, engages with regulators on CCTS and green steel taxonomy, and launched a Carbon Bank. In the UK, it builds a 3.2 MTPA EAF facility to cut emissions ~90%, enhance steel security, and use domestic scrap. In the Netherlands, it collaborates with the government on the Groen Staal Plan with KPIs on CO2, emissions, and community quality of life, and offers low-carbon products. India's decarbonisation plan up to 2030 includes a scrap-based EAF plant, more renewables, higher scrap in BOF, biochar/natural gas, and low-TRL pilots; up to 2045, it targets fully renewable power, hydrogen/gas-based DRI, gas injection in blast furnaces, green hydrogen, CCUS pilots, value-added products from captured carbon, and scaling HIsarna and EASyMelt. Nature strategy uses TNFD's LEAP approach, a nature interface map, impact assessments, six management levers, and time-bound targets with monitoring and disclosures.

Community engagement includes water projects, solar lights, climate-resilient agriculture, and species conservation. Opportunities cover green steel taxonomy, carbon credit trading, and low-carbon market offerings (Optemis®, Zeremis®). Actions include biochar use, renewable energy expansion, electric transport, carbon bank, rewilding, and transition to electric arc furnaces in India, the Netherlands, and the UK.

nodes.title: D Metrics and targets
nodes.summary: Tata Steel reports ESG metrics aligned with BRSR, GHG Protocol, IFRS S2, GBF, and UN SDGs. ESG performance is disclosed via the Business Responsibility and Sustainability Report and ESG Factsheet in its Integrated Report. Environmental metrics cover GHG emissions, non-GHG air pollutants, waste generation, disposal, reuse/recycling/recovery, water discharge, and water withdrawal in stress areas. Targets are detailed in the ESG Goals section of the Integrated Report FY2024-25. The text also references Naxtra Park, West Bokaro, pages 104-105.

nodes.title: Enabling every ability

It also presents Tata Steel's ESG fact sheets for FY2024-25, detailing production, CO2 emissions, air emissions, water consumption, and discharge across entities. Furthermore, it includes ESG factsheets from FY2020-21 to FY2024-25, covering environmental metrics, social and safety metrics, product sustainability, capital expenditure, HR data, CSR, governance, ethics, supply chain, intellectual capital, and ResponsibleSteel certification, with multi-year figures, units, footnotes, and KPI assurance.

nodes.title: Enabling every ability (intro)
nodes.summary: The text covers the Sabal Awards by Tata Steel Foundation, launched in 2019 to celebrate excellence among Persons with Disabilities (PwDs), reaching 28 states and 6 UTs, engaging over 3,000 PwDs. It details the Sabal programme's block saturation model in Jharkhand and Odisha, ensuring rights-based entitlements under the RPwD Act 2016, with Noamundi as the first fully linked block. nodes.title: NINL

nodes.title: Tata Steel Thailand

nodes.title: B. OPERATIONS
nodes.summary: This section covers Tata Steel's operational risks and mitigation approaches across health and safety, air quality, biodiversity, and supply chain sustainability, including financial implications. nodes.title: Tata Steel Operations: Health, Safety, and Air Quality Risks and Mitigation

References to further details in the Integrated Report are provided.

TSN targets 40% Scope 1 CO2 reduction by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2045, transitioning to DRI and electric smelting with green hydrogen, supported by government discussions. Carbon neutrality achieved at six sites, with an energy-efficient furnace in Maubeuge cutting energy 16.4% and carbon 24%. TSUK is implementing a £1.25bn EAF transition at Port Talbot, reducing carbon footprint >50% and domestic CO2 ~90%, with ISO 50001 certification and efficiency projects. TSUK engages in regional decarbonization clusters and hydrogen infrastructure.

nodes.title: 3. Health and Safety
nodes.summary: Tata Steel's health and safety commitment includes integrated management, board oversight, digital innovations, contractor safety, risk audits, and leadership programs. Recognized by World Steel for process safety, it conducts hazard studies and well-being initiatives. A '5 Safe Steps Forward' campaign and Consequence Management Policy enforce Life-Saving Rules. Indian operations saw a 17% LTI reduction but reported five fatalities. TSN's 'True Safe' program and ISO 45001 certification progress are noted, though LTIs rose 30%. TSUK achieved zero fatalities, 32% LTI reduction, and 20% fewer accidents, with ISO 45001 transition and health and safety plans focusing on decommissioning, process safety, and occupational health.

nodes.title: 4. Research and Development
nodes.summary: Tata Steel's R&D division drives sustainability and commercial success through product and process innovation. It collaborates with Imperial College London, Henry Royce Institute, IIT-ISM Dhanbad, and UK universities (Swansea, Warwick, Cambridge). Decarbonisation efforts include a green hydrogen project producing syngas/char from biomass and municipal waste via thermocatalytic gasification, piloted at Kalinganagar with 3 t CO2/t feed abatement potential; a two-step ferro manganese technology using sulphur reductant cutting CO2 by ~40% and producing sulfuric acid; and a chromate-free coating for Tata Structura GP tubes. It developed hydrogen-compliant API X65 ERW pipes qualified for 100% hydrogen at 100 bar. TSN's R&D allocates 89% to Research Portfolio Committees, 6% to Strategic Thrust programmes (e.g., HIsarna), and 5% to Direct Support. FY2024-25 process technology focused on stability and cost reduction, including DRI/scrap-EAF simulations, de-nitrogenation/desulphurisation trials, and a gas model saving up to €10 mn annually. Product innovations include Protact Trivalent Chromium-Coating for cans and improved Valast® bend performance. TSN is redesigning its new product development process for green steel, with Strategic Technology Roadmaps on scrap/slag/steelmaking, EAF recipes, coatings, and product applications. TSUK R&D headcount reduced ~80%, focusing on critical medium-to-long-term projects. UK collaborations include packaging steel concepts, annealing digital twins, high-strength packaging steel (patent pending), low-tin coating adhesion, can lid tools, multifunctional polymer barriers for hydrogen economy, automotive steel homologation, laser-weldability prediction, and trapped elements in EAF steelmaking. The Company participates in Flue2Chem (captured CO2 in paints, pilot at Shotton) and SUSTAIN consortia; TSUK's Sustainability Policy & Assessment team won worldsteel's Excellence in LCA Steelie Award 2024.

nodes.title: 5. New Product Development
nodes.summary: In FY2024-25, Tata Steel developed 123 new products across segments. Automotive innovations include CP780 steel, Tisten 52/55, SPFH590, and BSK46/E46 grades. For oil and gas, it produced hot-rolled steel for hydrogen transport and ERW pipes with Welspun. Lifting and excavation saw C15 substrate for ammunition and STK500/STK540 tubes for bullet train. Cold rolled/coated products included 17 dual-phase and interstitial-free steels. Long products featured 550D rebar, corrosion-resistant rebars, HC78ACr wire rod, and special bar quality grades for bearings, gears, and crankshafts. TSN launched 17 products, including HR-CP800 HyperFlange, solar panel steel, and color-coated products. TSUK launched five products, such as chrome-free passivation for tinplate, High Containment Barrier System, Trimapanel Fire Wall, and ComFlor FD+ decking. Focus also includes EAF and blast furnace route developments for future markets.

nodes.title: 6. Customer Relationship
nodes.summary: The text covers Tata Steel's FY2024-25 customer relationship initiatives, including AI and digital technology adoption to enhance customer experiences. It details investments in advanced facilities like the Continuous Annealing Line at Kalinganagar and new galvanising and Combi-Mill facilities. Product innovations include hydrogen-compliant steel, automotive-grade steels, shipbuilding plates, and Poly-Coated steel. Customer relationship strengthening spans B2B automotive, construction, and B2C segments with expanded service centres, training events, and consumer initiatives. Digital transformation includes Tata Steel Aashiyana, DigECA, COMPASS, and Nest-In platforms. TSN's green steel plan, CRM system, and digital platforms are highlighted, alongside TSUK's sustainability progress, low CO2 steel agreement with JCB, and product innovations like SolarSeam.

nodes.title: 7. Digital Transformation
nodes.summary: Tata Steel's digital transformation strategy focuses on cloud, data, and AI as value-driven enablers. It has invested in secure, multi-tenant cloud infrastructure, consolidated enterprise systems, and standardized global processes. The company has curated 11.2 Pb of data and implemented data quality management for a 'single version of truth.' Over 5-6 years, it developed 588 AI models, including generative AI, for automated insights and conversational interfaces. About 75% of these models drive manufacturing excellence (yield, energy efficiency, throughput, quality, productivity, safety) via science-based, ML, DL, vision, and generative AI, enabling remote and intelligent operations. Functional excellence in HR, procurement, finance, and supply chain/logistics is also boosted. Customer experience is enhanced with ~₹500 crore monthly online sales and 20% of AI models focused on interactions and complaint resolution. The Shikhar Value Framework delivers value; 80% of steel production comes from WEF Global Lighthouse sites, and Gartner recognized Tata Steel as an Advanced Leader in Digital for four consecutive years.

It discusses moderating global inflation (4.3% in 2025, 3.6% in 2026), divergent monetary policy, tightening fiscal policy in advanced economies, and moderate adjustments in developing economies. It provides regional outlooks: US growth at 1.5% with policy implications; Europe's 0.8% growth in 2024 and flat 2025; UK's 1.0% growth; China's 5% growth in 2024 and 4.5% projected for 2025-2026. nodes.title: 2. Indian Economy
nodes.summary: India's economy is among the fastest-growing, with 6.5% growth in FY2024-25 and projected 6-6.5% growth ahead, driven by domestic consumption, government capex, and services/manufacturing. Inflation is projected to moderate to 4.0-4.5%, enabling RBI rate cuts; FPI volatility is expected to subside and crude prices to soften. Services, construction, utilities, high-value manufacturing exports, and agriculture show resilience. Government focuses on fiscal consolidation, employment, capex, and PLI expansion. Downside risks include weaker investment, rupee depreciation, conflicts, trade policies, and supply disruptions. Outlook remains strong, aided by improved trade ties like the India-UK agreement.

nodes.title: 3. Global Steel Industry
nodes.summary: The text covers the global steel industry's challenges, including subdued manufacturing, high input costs, geopolitical uncertainty, and weak housing and automotive demand. It notes resilience in developing economies like India and rising Chinese exports, which triggered protectionist measures. It details 2024 demand declines in China, developed economies, and Europe, with projections for 2025 global growth of 1.2%, recovery outside China, and regional outlooks. Risks from US tariffs and China's real estate downturn are highlighted, alongside expected recoveries in developing economies, developed economies, and Europe, with government interventions potentially stabilizing demand.

nodes.title: 4. Indian Steel Industry
nodes.summary: India is the world’s second-largest steel producer, with demand projected to grow 8% in 2025 and reach 200-210 million tonnes by 2030, driven by infrastructure, housing, transportation, power, renewable energy, consumer durables, and capital goods. Government initiatives like PLI schemes, infrastructure investment, and maintained capex in the FY2025-26 Union Budget support growth. Steel prices remain range-bound due to Chinese import threats, partially eased by a 12% safeguard duty from April 21, 2025, for 200 days. While global demand recovers, geopolitical, economic, and financial risks persist; India remains a high-growth market with an optimistic long-term outlook, requiring effective trade policies, price stabilization, and sustained investment for competitiveness.

Tinplate is an eco-friendly packaging medium for edible oil, processed foods, and aerosol cans. Domestic demand grew ~4% in FY2024-25, driven by edible oil (~5%) and processed food (~4%), with paints improving. Production was 375 kt and sales 371 kt, flat versus FY2023-24. The division pursues operational improvements, a 300 KTPA expansion, Zero Effluent Discharge, cost efficiency, new product development, and completed an SA8000 semi-audit with continued certification recommendation.

nodes.title: d) Metaliks & Ductile Iron (DI) Pipes Division
nodes.summary: The Metaliks & Ductile Iron (DI) Pipes Division, merged with Tata Steel, operates in Kharagpur with 600 KT hot metal capacity, producing Pig Iron ('Tata eFee') and DI Pipes ('Tata Ductura'). Pig Iron demand was subdued due to reduced demand and Russian imports, but sales rose ~25% with over 90% market share in foundry-grade Pig Iron in eastern India. DI Pipe demand surged ~38% in FY2023-24, continued growth in H1 FY2024-25, then declined, with full-year demand up ~2%; price corrections of 15-20% are expected. The division expects ~13% delivery growth and market share rise from 11.5% to ~12.8%. Short-term outlook is weak, but medium-to-long-term is optimistic due to Jal Jeevan Mission and river linking projects. FY2024-25 production: ~584 KT hot metal (+17%), ~450 KT DI Pipes (+13%), ~152 KT Pig Iron (+26%). Deliveries: 150 KT Pig Iron (+23%), 452 KT DI Pipes (+14%). Three new CCMs and a finishing line were commissioned, dispatch/logistics improved, and a Zero Effluent Discharge project was completed.

nodes.title: e) Industrial By-Products and Management Division
nodes.summary: The Industrial By-products Management Division (IBMD) of Tata Steel promotes circular economy principles by extracting value from by-products across the steel value chain, managing over 25 product categories and 250+ SKUs for industries like cement, chemical, construction, infrastructure, and thermal power. In FY2024-25, IBMD handled ~17 million tonnes of by-products but saw an 11% revenue decline due to limited metallics availability and subdued markets. The division supplied 1.93 million tonnes of scrap internally, achieving a best-ever 1.45 million tonnes internal scrap supply and reducing external procurement by 33%. Value addition efforts included ramping up Flat Product processing, achieving best-ever sales of 343KT, commencing ACBF crushing and screening at TSM, and converting FHCR to black plate via EPA. Tata Dureco GGBS sales grew 1.5X with new EPA sites, used in major infrastructure projects. Tata Aggreto and Tata Nirman sales grew, used in national highways and rural road projects. IBMD made its first export sale of Crude Benzol from TSM. Tata Steel received the RASHTA Award for Best Use of Waste Material Recycling in Road Construction.

nodes.title: f) Ferro Alloys and Minerals Division
nodes.summary: The text covers Tata Steel's Ferro Alloys and Minerals Division (FAMD) and Bearings Division. FAMD is a leading producer of Ferro Chrome and Manganese alloys with integrated facilities across four Indian states, captive plants, and business-partnered Ferro Processing Centres. It operates three chromite and four manganese mines, and has applied to surrender the Sukinda Chromite Mine. Production and sales data from FY21 to FY25 are provided, including Tata Steel Mining Limited post-merger. FY2024-25 highlights include focus on value-added products, development of low-silicon ferrochrome markets, lower production due to reduced chrome ore output, and lower deliveries due to higher royalty rates and dampened global steel sentiments. Achievements include low-phosphorus ferrochrome trials, 112 tons of premium low-silicon ferrochrome shipped to Rotterdam, and awards for sustainable technologies and safety. The Bearings Division, based in Kharagpur, has ~40 million annual capacity, IATF 16949 and ISO 45001 certifications, and serves OE and aftermarket segments. Production and sales data from FY21 to FY25 are given. FY2024-25 highlights include ~36 million bearings produced and delivered (up 2 million), best-ever aftermarket sales of 7.04 million bearings, EV bearing development expanded to commercial vehicles with Tata Motors, and launch of the 'Kriyaveer' skill transition program.

nodes.title: b) Marketing and Sales
nodes.summary: The text details Tata Steel's FY2024-25 marketing and sales performance, with total deliveries of 20.94 MT (5% Y-o-Y growth). It covers three segments: Automotive & Special Products (18% of domestic sales) with 3.1 MT deliveries, maintaining leadership via new high-strength steel products, CAL commissioning, and awards; Branded Products & Retail (40% of domestic sales) achieving ~7 MT sales (7% growth), highlighting Tata Astrum/Steelium record sales, Tata Tiscon rebar growth, and Aashiyana e-commerce platform; and Industrial Products, Projects & Exports (42% of domestic sales) with record engineering sales, foray into shipbuilding, hydrogen-grade pipes, and construction solutions. It also covers digital initiatives like QR feedback, TSL CARes, COMPASS, DigECA, and Aashiyana's NPS improvement. The summary emphasizes strategic initiatives, innovation, and market leadership.

nodes.title: c) Engineering & Projects
nodes.summary: The Engineering & Projects Division had a remarkable FY2024-25, commissioning critical projects including the Kalinganagar expansion (3 to 8 MTPA) with India's largest blast furnace, coke plant, and various facilities. It commissioned raw material facilities at Noamundi and Joda, and made progress on the EAF project at Ludhiana for decarbonization. Milestones included a 6 MTPA Iron Ore Processing Plant, railway siding at Joda, new hospitals, a structural tube mill, and a bio-oxidation plant. At Kalinganagar, BF#2, CETP, continuous annealing line, coke battery, ASU, solar project, and rail infrastructure were commissioned. At Meramandali, CDQ, dust extraction systems, and a command control centre were completed. The division received three INVEST awards. Financially, profit after tax was ₹13,970 crore, down from ₹15,662 crore due to lower steel prices from cheap imports, partly offset by higher sales volume and lower raw material costs. Revenue from operations decreased by 6% to ₹1,32,517 crore, with sale of products down 6% and power/water and other operating revenue also lower. Purchases of stock-in-trade marginally increased by 1% to ₹9,825 crore due to higher traded rebars, partly offset by lower external scrap purchases.

nodes.title: 2. Neelachal Ispat Nigam Limited
nodes.summary: The text covers Neelachal Ispat Nigam Limited (NINL), acquired by Tata Steel in July 2022, located in Kalinganagar, Odisha. It details NINL's primary product (long products like rebar), collaboration with Tata Steel for rebar production and Tiscon brand introduction. Financials for FY2024-25 vs FY2023-24 include turnover, EBITDA, PBT, and PAT, along with production and sales performance (crude steel, saleable steel, sales). It highlights production ramp-up, pig iron decline, steel delivery increase, turnover and EBITDA improvement, and reduced loss after tax. Year under review achievements include record productions in crude steel, hot metal, rebar, power, and sinter. Cost reduction initiatives (process solid waste utilization, leaner coal blend) are noted. Financial highlights include highest-ever EBITDA and free cash flow crossing ₹1,000 crore. Strategy focuses on transforming NINL into a state-of-the-art long products complex with captive iron ore mines. Safety and sustainability covers ISO:14001 certification, consent for coal injection system, safety awards, enhanced product mix approval, and vendor incentivisation scheme.

nodes.title: 3. Tata Steel Downstream Products Limited
nodes.summary: Tata Steel Downstream Products Limited (TSDPL) is a leader in the flat products steel service centre business, acting as a bridge between steel producers and end-customers with a pan-India presence. It offers processing and value-added services like just-in-time delivery, inventory management, slitting, and fabrication. The text covers TSDPL's financial performance for FY2024-25, including turnover and profit figures, and discusses challenging market conditions due to declining steel prices and lower automotive demand. It details the company's performance under six strategic priorities: Safety & Sustainability (improving injury rates, environmental initiatives, CSR impacting 75,000+ lives), Customer (expanding product basket, onboarding channel finance partners, reducing complaint resolution time), Growth (adding processing capacity, new facilities), Operational Excellence (Lakshya 2.0 program, EBITDA savings), Digital & Innovation (DigiYaan program, digital tools), and People (diversity, training). It also mentions awards received by its plants.

nodes.title: 4. Europe Operations
nodes.summary: The text covers Tata Steel's Europe operations for FY2024-25, detailing turnover, EBITDA, PBT, and PAT losses compared to FY2023-24. It reports liquid steel production and deliveries, noting a slight increase in deliveries due to higher production in the Netherlands. The narrative explains the EBITDA loss reduction, driven by improved TSN performance after Blast Furnace 6 reline, while TSUK had higher losses due to asset closures. For Tata Steel Netherlands (TSN), it discusses operational challenges, environmental concerns, stakeholder engagement, cost-saving measures, and progress on the DRI transition and 'Maatwerk' support. For Tata Steel UK (TSUK), it covers the closure of primary steelmaking, lower production and deliveries, the Grant Funding Agreement for EAF steelmaking, planning approval, and cost control programs.

nodes.title: 5. Tata Steel Thailand (TSTH)
nodes.summary: Tata Steel Thailand (TSTH) reported FY2024-25 Thailand steel consumption at 16.3 MT (-0.2% YoY), with imports at 11.4 MT (69.9% of demand, +1.7% YoY). Long product consumption was 6.23 MT (+0.6% YoY), imports 2.89 MT (46.4% of demand, +9.9% YoY), with continuous imports from China and ASEAN, especially wire rods. Thai GDP grew 2.5% in 2024 (vs 2.0% in 2023) but below expectations, with a ~15% fall in equities; 2025 GDP projected at 2.3-3.3%, supported by government spending, private consumption, tourism, and exports, but risks from U.S. trade protection. Domestic deliveries were lower due to competition in rebars and higher wire rod imports, offset by increased exports. Financials: turnover ₹6,055 crore (FY25) vs ₹5,829 crore (FY24); EBITDA ₹106 crore vs ₹44 crore; PBT before exceptional ₹38 crore vs ₹(30) crore; PBT ₹101 crore vs ₹22 crore; PAT before exceptional ₹18 crore vs ₹(29) crore; PAT ₹81 crore vs ₹23 crore. Production and sales: saleable steel production 1.19 MT vs 1.12 MT (+6%); sales 1.19 MT vs 1.12 MT (+7%). Turnover increased by ₹227 crore due to higher deliveries; PAT up ₹58 crore from higher operating profits and one-time land sale gain. Year under review: completed 11 MW solar roof project saving ~20 MB annually; highest export sales of 244 kt (20% of total sales volume); monetized unused land assets. Recognitions: ESG Rating Rank A from SET; improved corporate governance score. Safety, Health & Environment: TSMT-SCSC and SISCO received Excellent Practices Establishment on Occupational Safety & Health certificates; TSMT-NTS, SCSC, SISCO received Green Star Award 2024 Level 4.

nodes.title: 6. The Siam Industrial Wire Co. Ltd. (‘SIW’) & TSN Wires Co. Ltd. (‘TSN Wires’)
nodes.summary: The text profiles Siam Industrial Wire (SIW), a leading Thai steel wire manufacturer specializing in PC Strand, PC Wire, Wire Mesh, and Cold Drawn Wires, holding 34% market share in PC Strand/Wire and exporting to over 70 countries, and its 60% subsidiary TSN Wires, which produces galvanised wires for fencing, poultry, farming, and paper pulp, leading Thailand's market with 47% share. It notes public sector project delays, stable TSN galvanised wire business, export challenges from Chinese oversupply and trade barriers (Vietnam anti-dumping, US Section 232 duties), and carbon emission requirements. Financial data for FY2024-25 show SIW turnover ₹1,431 crore (up from ₹1,416 crore) with lower profits, and TSN turnover ₹275 crore (up from ₹251 crore) with a loss. Production/sales figures are provided. Combined saleable steel production decreased 1% and deliveries rose 5%, with turnover up 2% but profits declined. The review highlights TSN's first sales to renewable energy, low emission steel launch, and recognitions including LESS certification, ISO/IEC 27001, and an occupational safety award.

nodes.title: 7. Tata Steel Minerals Canada (TSMC)
nodes.summary: Tata Steel Minerals Canada (TSMC), a partnership between Tata Steel (82%) and the Government of Quebec (18%), mines and processes high-grade iron ore from hematite deposits in the Menihek region near Schefferville. It produces sinter fines and superfine material with minimum 64% Fe, and DSO with 60-62% Fe, railed to Sept-Îles for global shipping. FY2024-25 saw iron ore price fluctuations due to decreased global steel demand, particularly in China, with recovery later from stimulus measures. Global shipping costs surged due to disruptions in the Red Sea, Panama Canal, and Suez Canal, later subsiding. Financials show turnover of ₹1,422 crore (up 7% from ₹1,330 crore) and increased loss before tax of ₹1,457 crore (from ₹771 crore) due to lower prices, inventory provisions, and higher finance costs. Production reached ~3 MT of iron ore fines (up ~35%) with total shipments of ~2.4 MT, achieving 100% compliance on Fe and silica content with zero quality penalties. TSMC received the Tata North America Sustainability Award for environmental conservation, carbon reduction, and water management involving local Indigenous communities. Consolidated profit after tax was ₹3,174 crore versus a loss of ₹4,910 crore, aided by lower EBITDA loss in the Netherlands, improved NINL profits, and prior-year exceptional charges. Basic and diluted earnings per share were ₹2.74 (previous year loss: ₹3.62).

nodes.title: VIII. Risks and Concerns
nodes.summary: The section covers Tata Steel's comprehensive risk landscape and mitigation strategies. Macroeconomic and market risks from global challenges, China's property sector, and demand/pricing pressures are met with domestic focus, high-value products, and policy advocacy. Regulatory risks from protectionism, tariffs, and CBAM are mitigated through compliance and engagement. Commodity risk covers coal and bulk procurement, market trends, and supply chain vulnerabilities, with strategies like hedging, diversification, and infrastructure investment. Operational risks include supply chain disruptions, cybersecurity, equipment failures, and safety hazards, addressed via maintenance consolidation, IoT, safety programs, and community initiatives. Cyber and information security risks from IT reliance and digital transformation are mitigated with advanced security measures, governance, and continuous technology refresh.

nodes.title: Tata Steel Risks, ERM Governance, Financial Risk and Mitigation
nodes.summary: The page outlines Tata Steel’s risks and concerns in a dynamic global environment, covering regulatory, environmental, geopolitical, and technological exposures. It describes the Enterprise Risk Management framework and governance structure, including Board and senior management committees. It details Financial Risk: capacity expansion in India, UK transition to Electric Arc Furnace, TSN decarbonisation, substantial upfront and decommissioning costs, net debt of ₹82,579 crore as of March 31, 2025, funding through internal accruals and external capital, sensitivity to interest rates, ESG factors, commodity and currency volatility, and working capital impacts. Mitigation Strategies include cash flow generation, working capital optimisation, continuous improvement, portfolio restructuring, high-return projects, diversified funding, government grants for green initiatives, longer-term flexible debt, ESG collaboration with TCFD, investor engagement, and the ‘One Treasury’ approach for group-wide treasury, cashflow, currency, and commodity hedging management.

nodes.title: Macroeconomic and Market Risk
nodes.summary: The text covers macroeconomic and market risks in FY2024-25, including global economic challenges, steel industry impacts from China's property sector, and demand/pricing pressures in India, UK, and Netherlands. It details mitigation strategies: focusing on the domestic Indian market with automotive leadership, construction solutions, engineering growth, branded sales, localisation, and continuous improvement. For Tata Steel Netherlands, strategies include high-value products, portfolio optimisation, and policy advocacy on CBAM. Regulatory risks from protectionism, tariffs, and environmental laws are discussed, along with mitigation through compliance systems and policy engagement.

nodes.title: Steel Industry Mitigation Strategies and Regulatory Risk Management
nodes.summary: The text covers mitigation strategies addressing pricing pressures from sluggish steel demand, climate compliance costs, and imports, focusing on India's domestic market with automotive leadership, construction solutions, engineering growth, branded sales, localisation, and continuous improvement. It details Tata Steel Netherlands and UK strategies for high-value products, portfolio optimization, CBAM advocacy, and green steel, plus expected benefits from safeguard duties. Regulatory risk covers the dynamic global regulatory environment, protectionism, tariffs, Section 232, and CBAM. Mitigation includes proactive regulatory monitoring, compliance systems, environmental stewardship, and policy advocacy.

nodes.title: Mitigation Strategies
nodes.summary: The text covers statutory reporting on market pressures in the UK and Netherlands from sluggish steel demand, climate compliance costs, and imports. Mitigation strategies include focusing on India's domestic market with automotive leadership (new Continuous Annealing Line), construction solutions (31 service centres, Plate Fabricated Sections), engineering growth (railways, yellow goods, hydrogen pipes), branded sales growth (Tata Tiscon, Tata Steelium), localisation (CP780, Poly Steel), and continuous improvement (Shikhar). Tata Steel Netherlands and UK prioritize high-value products, green steel, and CBAM advocacy. Regulatory risks include protectionism, tariffs, and CBAM; mitigation involves compliance systems, policy advocacy, safeguard duties, R&D for decarbonisation, and government engagement (e.g., £500 million EAF grant).

nodes.title: Commodity Risk
nodes.summary: The text covers commodity risk for Tata Steel, noting coal and bulk commodities make up 61% of procurement. It details FY2024-25 market trends: stable global steel and met coal demand, coking coal prices hitting a four-year low in March 2025 due to reduced imports, slower steel production growth, increased supply from China and Indonesia, and trade tensions/sanctions causing volatility. Chinese steel prices eased while iron ore remained stable. It lists external and internal risks: dependence on Australia for seaborne met coal, logistics challenges in Indonesia and Mozambique, extreme weather and geopolitical events, high reliance on South Africa for DRI thermal coal, NRS auctions and road movement impacting inventory, process consumable price volatility from Chinese sentiment, and changing statutory/sustainability norms threatening supply chain reliability.

nodes.title: Mitigation Strategies
nodes.summary: The text outlines Tata Steel's mitigation strategies for raw material price volatility, supply chain risks, and operational risks. For price volatility, strategies include group-wide hedging, price forecasting, reverse auctions, captive raw materials, coal sourcing diversification, long-term contracts, trial of new coal grades, and exploring new sources. Supply chain risks are addressed through port infrastructure debottlenecking, railway infrastructure investment, cost optimization, and sustainability initiatives like biofuel and LNG vessels. Operational risks include external threats like extreme weather and cybersecurity, and internal issues like equipment failures. The text also covers indigenization, sustainable procurement, and the scale of Tata Steel's supply chain.

nodes.title: Tata Steel Supply Chain Risks and Mitigation Strategies
nodes.summary: The page covers Tata Steel's supply chain risk and mitigation strategies. Risks include complex global supply chains, infrastructure strain from capacity expansion in East India, railway and port disruptions, cost-adverse freight policies, geopolitical tensions affecting shipping, and stringent ESG norms. Mitigation strategies involve local rake contracts, Fuel Supply Agreements, indigenization for de-risking, sustainable procurement, port debottlenecking, railway infrastructure investment, cost optimization via commercial levers and hedging, and sustainability initiatives like biofuel and LNG vessels, and alternative fuel vehicles.

nodes.title: Operational Risk
nodes.summary: The text covers operational risks in the steel industry, including external supply chain disruptions, cybersecurity threats, equipment failures, aging assets, and utility disruptions. Mitigation strategies include consolidated maintenance, real-time asset monitoring, an Integrated Maintenance Excellence Centre, smart indenting, predictive maintenance via IoT, cost optimization, and facility upgrades. It details Tata Steel UK's transition to an Electric Arc Furnace, an MoU with JCB, improvements at IJmuiden, and a Corporate Asset Management Framework. Drone-based gas line monitoring, power system restructuring, spare parts indigenisation, and a disaster response plan are also addressed. Safety risks and mitigation strategies are outlined, focusing on a 'Committed to Zero' objective, safety management, behavioral safety, business continuity, hazard studies, audits, process safety management, and skill development.

nodes.title: Tata Steel Mitigation Strategies and Safety Risk
nodes.summary: Mitigation covers manufacturing cost disruptions from utility failures, consolidated maintenance across India with real-time monitoring, i-MEC, smart indenting, IoT and condition-based maintenance, cost optimization, vendor synergy, and Jamshedpur facility upgrades. It also includes Tata Steel UK's EAF transition, blast furnace shutdowns, substrate imports, JCB MoU, IJmuiden structural improvements, and TSN asset management. Gas line safety uses drone monitoring; power restructuring ensures availability. Indigenisation of spares addresses geopolitical supply uncertainty. A disaster response plan covers extreme weather and pandemics. Safety Risk addresses industry hazards, non-compliance, and geographic complexity, mitigated by 'Committed to Zero', standardised policy, behavioral safety, Business Continuity Management, PSSR audits, PSM assessment, vendor-inclusive safety rewards, and risk perception training.

nodes.title: Mitigation Strategies
nodes.summary: The text covers mitigation strategies for operational risks: maintenance consolidation, real-time monitoring, i-MEC, smart indenting, predictive analytics, and UK EAF transition with JCB MoU. It addresses spare part indigenisation, disaster response, and safety risks with 'Committed to Zero', behavioural safety, PSSR audits, and safety campaigns. Community risk mitigation includes Tata Steel Foundation's education, health, sports, tribal, disability, water, infrastructure, and empowerment programs; UK community partnership; and Netherlands decarbonisation. Cyber and information security risk is mentioned but details are truncated.

nodes.title: Tata Steel Safety, Community Risk, and Mitigation Strategies
nodes.summary: The page covers statutory safety initiatives in India and the UK, including skill upgrades, awareness campaigns (5 Safe Steps Forward, Road Safety Month, National Safety Week, National Fire Service Week), road safety technology, and programmes like Process Safety Alerts, Know Your PPE, Monsoon Safety Tips, Timeout for Safety, and TrueSafe. It addresses community risks from noise, dust, and emissions, especially in the Netherlands, and mitigation strategies: Tata Steel Foundation's social impact programmes in India (education, health, sports, tribal identity, disability, water conservation, infrastructure, gender empowerment) impacting 5.77 million lives, UK community partnerships and economic regeneration, and Netherlands decarbonisation exceeding legal standards.

nodes.title: Cyber and Information Security Risk
nodes.summary: The Company's heavy reliance on IT and digital transformation, including AI, robotics, and machine learning, drives growth but heightens cyber and privacy risks, regulatory non-compliance, faulty data, and performance instability. It emphasizes protecting organizational data for confidentiality, integrity, and availability under data governance norms, and complying with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 to avoid penalties and reputational harm. Additionally, it stresses addressing technology obsolescence to mitigate cyber and business continuity risks.

nodes.title: Mitigation Strategies

nodes.title: Development expenditure for mineral reserves
nodes.summary:
Development expenditure for mineral reserves
Development is the establishment of access to mineral reserves and other preparations for commercial production. Development activities often continue during production and include:
• sinking shafts and underground drifts (often called mine development)
• making permanent excavations
• developing passageways and rooms or galleries
• building roads and tunnels and
• advance removal of overburden and waste rock.
Development (or construction) also includes the installation of infrastructure (e.g., roads, utilities and housing), machinery, equipment and facilities.
Development expenditure is capitalised and presented as part of mining assets. No depreciation is charged on the development expenditure before the start of commercial production.

nodes.title: Provision for restoration and environmental costs
nodes.summary: The text outlines the accounting policy for restoration and environmental costs, covering liabilities for soil restoration due at mining site closures. It explains that liabilities are estimated case-by-case per local legal requirements, using current technology and prices, and discounted for time value when material. Future costs are capitalized at net present value, with corresponding liabilities raised when obligations arise. Capitalized costs are depreciated over the asset's life, and the time value effect is recognized in profit and loss.

nodes.title: (i) Stripping Costs
nodes.summary: The text distinguishes developmental and production stripping costs in surface mining. Developmental costs, incurred to access future mineral reserves, are capitalized as mining assets until commercial production begins. Accounting for multiple open pits depends on whether they are separate or integrated operations, based on factors like mining sequence, investment decisions, operational planning, infrastructure expenditure, and ore body distinctness. Production stripping costs are incurred to extract ore or improve access, and are accounted for as inventories or as a stripping activity asset if future economic benefits are probable, the ore body component is identifiable, and costs are reliably measurable. Stripping activity assets are carried at cost less amortization and impairment, using the useful life of the identified ore body component.

nodes.title: Financial assets measured at fair value
nodes.summary: The text outlines accounting policies for financial assets and liabilities. It covers measurement of financial assets at fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI) based on business model and cash flow characteristics, including irrevocable election for equity investments held for strategic purposes. It details interest and dividend income recognition, impairment via expected credit losses (lifetime for trade receivables, 12-month or lifetime for others based on credit risk increase), and de-recognition criteria for financial assets. It also addresses classification of financial liabilities and equity instruments by substance, measurement of equity instruments at proceeds net of costs, and initial and subsequent measurement of trade payables and borrowings at fair value and amortized cost using effective interest method.

nodes.title: Material Accounting Policies: Financial Instruments and Equity
nodes.summary: This page outlines material accounting policies for financial instruments. It covers recognition of interest income on a time-proportion basis and dividend income when the right to receive is established. Impairment of financial assets is detailed, including expected credit loss allowances for amortised cost and fair value through other comprehensive income assets, with lifetime or twelve-month allowances based on credit risk changes. De-recognition criteria for financial assets are explained. The page also addresses classification of financial liabilities and equity instruments by contractual substance, defines equity instruments, and describes initial and subsequent measurement of financial liabilities.

nodes.title: Financial liabilities
nodes.summary: The text outlines material accounting policies for financial statements, covering financial assets classification and measurement (including amortized cost, fair value through other comprehensive income for strategic equity investments, and fair value through profit/loss), interest and dividend income recognition, impairment of financial assets via expected credit losses (with lifetime vs. 12-month recognition based on credit risk changes), and de-recognition criteria. It also covers financial liabilities and equity instruments classification, initial and subsequent measurement of payables and borrowings, de-recognition of financial liabilities, and derivative financial instruments and hedge accounting, including types of derivatives used, hedge documentation, effectiveness assessment, accounting for fair value and cash flow hedges, and hedge discontinuation. A reference to note 37 for further details is included.

nodes.title: Financial Liabilities and Derivative Hedge Accounting Policies
key_items: Derivative financial instruments and hedge accounting
nodes.summary: This page covers material accounting policies: measurement of financial liabilities at amortized cost using the effective interest rate method, with differences between proceeds and settlement recognized over the borrowing term. It details de-recognition of financial liabilities when obligations are discharged, cancelled, or expire. It also covers derivative financial instruments and hedge accounting, including the use of forwards, swaps, and collars to hedge foreign exchange, base metal price, and interest rate risks; initial and subsequent fair value measurement; adoption of hedge accounting with formal documentation, effectiveness assessment at inception and ongoing, and immediate recognition of ineffective portions in profit and loss.

nodes.title: When hedge accounting is applied:
nodes.summary: The text covers hedge accounting application for fair value and cash flow hedges, including recognition of gains/losses, ineffective portions, non-financial asset adjustments, and deferral in equity. It explains discontinuation of hedge accounting and treatment of cumulative gains/losses. It also details employee benefits: defined contribution plans expensed as services rendered; defined benefit plans using Projected Unit Credit Method with actuarial valuation, remeasurements in OCI, service cost and net interest as expenses, and past service cost recognition; compensated absences measured at present value using projected unit credit method, with actuarial gains/losses in profit and loss. Inventories comprise raw materials, work-in-progress, finished/semi-finished goods, stock-in-trade, and stores/spares, recorded at lower of cost (weighted average) and net realisable value, with provisions for slow-moving/obsolete items. Provisions are recognised for present obligations, including decommissioning, site restoration, and environmental provisions, based on best estimate and discounted where material.

nodes.title: Employee Benefits Accounting Policies
nodes.summary: The page outlines material accounting policies for employee benefits, covering defined contribution plans, defined benefit plans, and compensated absences. Defined contribution plan contributions are expensed as services are rendered, with state-managed schemes treated similarly. Defined benefit plan costs use the Projected Unit Credit Method with annual actuarial valuation; remeasurement gains/losses go to other comprehensive income, while service cost and net interest are expensed. Past service cost is recognized when plan amendments or curtailments occur or when related restructuring or termination benefits are recognized. Balance sheet obligations reflect present value of defined benefit obligations less plan assets fair value. Compensated absences, including annual and sick leave, are measured at present value of estimated future cash outflows using the projected unit credit method with actuarial valuation; actuarial gains/losses are charged or credited to profit and loss. Absences not expected within twelve months are recognized based on actuarial valuation.

nodes.title: Inventories Inventories comprise the followings:
nodes.summary: The text covers material accounting policies: inventories (types, valuation at lower of cost and net realizable value, cost methods, provisions for slow-moving/obsolete items); provisions (recognition criteria, decommissioning/site restoration/environmental, best estimate, discounting, constructive obligation definition); onerous contracts (provision when expected benefits lower than unavoidable costs, measured at present value of lower of termination or continuation cost, impairment first); government grants (fair value recognition, conditions, asset-related grants credited over useful lives, deferred income); income taxes (current tax based on taxable profit, deferred tax using balance sheet liability method, recognition of deferred tax assets/liabilities, offsetting); revenue (sale of products recognized on control transfer, volume/price discounts estimated, no financing element for 30-90 day credit terms, refund provisions, receivables; sale of power based on approved tariff); foreign currency transactions (functional currency Indian Rupee, translation of monetary/non-monetary items, exchange differences in profit or loss); recent accounting pronouncements (amendments to Ind AS 117 and Ind AS 116, no significant impact). Property, plant and equipment: detailed cost, impairment, depreciation, and net carrying value schedules for 2025 and 2024 across asset classes; notes on buildings held through shares, net carrying value of furniture/fixtures/office equipment, capitalized borrowing costs (8.24%), impairment testing (including Sukinda Chromite Block), pledged assets, CWIP additions, title deeds not held in company name with details of properties, gross carrying value, held-in-name entities, period held, and reasons; ageing of CWIP (less than 1 year to more than 3 years); expected completion of overdue CWIP by project category; capital cost of in-house research facilities.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Business Combinations and Consolidation Principles
key_items: Allocation of consideration over the fair value of assets and liabilities acquired in a business combination
nodes.summary: The page outlines material accounting policies, including assumptions for retirement benefit obligations reviewed annually with actuarial advice and referenced in note 36. It details the allocation of consideration in business combinations, where acquired assets and liabilities are stated at fair value on the acquisition date, estimated by independent valuers based on useful lives and expected benefits, with other assets/liabilities at expected realizable/settlement values. The basis of consolidation section explains that consolidated financial statements include the Company and controlled subsidiaries, plus share of profits, net assets, and reserves of joint arrangements and associates using equity or proportionate methods. It defines control, associates (significant influence, typically >20% voting rights), and joint arrangements (joint ventures and operations), including equity method accounting, loss limitation, and treatment of acquisitions/disposals. Intra-group transactions are eliminated, and non-controlling interests are presented separately.

nodes.title: (e) Business combinations
nodes.summary: The text details the accounting policy for business combinations, covering the acquisition method: consideration transferred measured at fair value of assets transferred, liabilities incurred, and equity interests issued; acquisition-related costs recognized in profit or loss; goodwill recognition as excess of consideration over net fair value of identifiable assets, liabilities, and contingent liabilities, with excess fair value over cost recognized as capital reserve; non-controlling interest initially measured at fair value or proportionate share, chosen per acquisition, and subsequently adjusted for share of equity changes, with comprehensive income attributed even if deficit; and post-control acquisitions of non-controlling interests treated as share purchases without further fair value adjustments, with any difference between cost and net book value adjusted in equity.

nodes.title: (f) Goodwill
nodes.summary: Goodwill is recognized at cost and measured at cost less accumulated impairment losses. It is allocated to cash-generating units (CGUs) for impairment testing, which occurs annually or more frequently if impairment indicators exist. Recoverable amount is the higher of fair value less costs to sell and value in use. Future cash flow projections consider economic uncertainties, discount rates, growth rates for terminal value, and sensitivity analysis. If recoverable amount is less than carrying value, impairment loss is first allocated to reduce goodwill, then to other assets proportionately.

nodes.title: (g) Property, plant and equipment
nodes.summary: This accounting policy covers property, plant and equipment measurement at cost or deemed cost less depreciation and impairment, including capitalization of direct costs, trial run expenses, and borrowing costs. Depreciation is straight-line over estimated useful lives, with regular reviews, and specific lives are listed for asset categories like buildings, roads, plant, machinery, furniture, vehicles, aircraft, railway sidings, and Electricity Act assets. Assets under construction are depreciated when ready for use. Impairment testing is described, including recoverable amount determination for individual assets or cash-generating units, and impairment loss recognition. Mining assets are amortized over mine life or lease period, with unit-of-production method for certain assets. Major furnace relining expenses are depreciated over 10 years, and freehold land is not depreciated. Useful lives for some assets differ from Companies Act requirements based on internal and independent technical evaluation.

nodes.title: (h) Exploration for and evaluation of mineral resources
nodes.summary: The text addresses accounting for exploration and evaluation of mineral resources, including recognizing expenditures as assets. It details cost components: acquiring rights, researching data, geological studies, drilling, sampling, extraction testing, and feasibility studies, plus evaluating technical and commercial viability. Administration costs are capitalized only if directly related; non-viable projects are written off. Assets are measured at cost, classified as property, plant, equipment, or intangible assets, with consumed tangible assets capitalized into intangibles. Capitalized exploration assets are not depreciated but monitored for impairment. Reclassification to mining assets occurs when technical feasibility and commercial viability are demonstrable and development is sanctioned by management.

nodes.title: (i) Development expenditure for mineral reserves
nodes.summary:
(i) Development expenditure for mineral reserves
Development is the establishment of access to mineral reserves and other preparations for commercial production. Development activities often continue during production and include:
• sinking shafts and underground drifts (often called mine development)
• making permanent excavations
• developing passageways and rooms or galleries
• building roads and tunnels and
• advance removal of overburden and waste rock.
Development (or construction) also includes the installation of infrastructure (e.g., roads, utilities and housing), machinery, equipment and facilities.

nodes.title: Provision for restoration and environmental costs
nodes.summary:
Provision for restoration and environmental costs
The Group has liabilities related to restoration of soil and other related works, which are due upon the closure of certain of its mining sites.
Such liabilities are estimated on a case-by-case based on available information, considering applicable local legal requirements. The estimation is made using existing technology, at current prices, and discounted using an appropriate discount rate where the effect of time value of money is material. Future restoration and environmental costs, discounted to net present value, are capitalised and the corresponding restoration liability is raised as soon as the obligation to incur such costs arises. Future restoration and environmental costs are capitalised in property, plant and equipment or mining assets as appropriate and are depreciated over the life of the related asset. The effect of time value of money on the restoration and environmental costs liability is recognised in the consolidated statement of profit and loss.

nodes.title: Stripping costs

It also details intangible assets (patents, trademarks, software, etc.) with useful lives, initial measurement, amortization, impairment testing, and business combination recognition. Finally, it addresses leases, including lessee accounting: identifying leases, separating lease and non-lease components, recognizing right-of-use assets and lease liabilities, measurement, depreciation, impairment, and remeasurement of lease liabilities.

nodes.title: Material Accounting Policies: Leases and Intangible Assets

It covers leases, including capitalization of stripping activity assets within mining assets, their initial and subsequent measurement, and depreciation based on the ore body's useful life. It also explains the criteria for identifying a lease: dependence on a specific asset and the right to control its use for payment. For intangible assets, it details recognition of patents, trademarks, and software when future economic benefits are probable, initial measurement at purchase cost, and straight-line amortization over estimated useful lives, with specified lives of up to 8 years for computer software, 4 years for patents and trademarks, and 5 years for product and process development costs and other intangible assets.

nodes.title: The Group as lessee

It also addresses lessor accounting for operating and finance leases, including income recognition and initial direct costs. Additionally, it outlines financial instruments accounting, covering initial recognition at fair value, transaction costs, subsequent measurement of financial assets at amortized cost or fair value, and classification of cash and bank balances.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Lessor, Financial Instruments, and Amortised Cost
nodes.summary: The page covers material accounting policies: lessor accounting distinguishes operating leases (straight-line rental income, initial direct costs added to asset) and finance leases (present value of minimum lease payments as receivable, unearned finance income, net investment method). It also covers financial instruments: initial recognition at fair value, treatment of transaction costs (capitalised or expensed for fair value through profit or loss), trade receivables measured at transaction price. Financial assets include cash and bank balances (cash equivalents with original maturities under three months, unrestricted; other bank balances restricted) and financial assets at amortised cost, measured subsequently at amortised cost if held within a business model to collect contractual cash flows that are solely payments of principal and interest.

nodes.title: Financial assets measured at fair value
nodes.summary: The text covers financial assets measured at fair value, detailing classification into fair value through other comprehensive income (FVOCI) for assets held to collect contractual cash flows and sell, and the irrevocable election for non-trading equity investments for medium/long-term strategic purposes. It explains interest and dividend income recognition, impairment of financial assets (expected credit losses for amortized cost and FVOCI assets, including lifetime ECL for trade receivables and credit risk assessment), and de-recognition criteria based on transfer of risks and rewards. It also addresses financial liabilities and equity instruments, including classification by substance, equity instruments recorded at proceeds net of costs, and financial liabilities (trade payables and interest-bearing loans) measured initially at fair value and subsequently at amortized cost using the effective interest rate method.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies for Financial Assets, Liabilities and Equity
nodes.summary: The page covers material accounting policies for financial instruments. It addresses equity investments designated at fair value through other comprehensive income, and financial assets measured at fair value through profit or loss. It details interest income recognition on a time-proportion basis and dividend income recognition when the right to receive payment is established. Impairment of financial assets includes expected credit loss allowances: lifetime for trade receivables without financing, twelve months for assets with no significant credit risk increase, and lifetime for assets with significantly increased credit risk. De-recognition of financial assets occurs when contractual cash flow rights expire or risks and rewards are substantially transferred, with specific treatment for partial transfer or retention. It also covers classification of financial liabilities and equity instruments as debt or equity based on contractual substance, equity instruments recorded at proceeds net of issue costs, and financial liabilities initially at fair value and subsequently at amortised cost.

nodes.title: Financial Liabilities
nodes.summary: The text outlines material accounting policies for financial instruments. It covers classification and measurement of equity investments irrevocably elected at fair value through OCI, and residual financial assets at fair value through P&L. It details interest income accrual, dividend recognition, and impairment via expected credit losses (lifetime for trade receivables, 12-month or lifetime based on credit risk changes). De-recognition rules for financial assets address expiry of rights, transfer of risks/rewards, and continuing involvement. It also covers classification of financial liabilities and equity, initial and subsequent measurement of payables and borrowings at amortised cost, and de-recognition of liabilities. Finally, it describes derivative instruments used for hedging foreign exchange, commodity, and interest rate risks, hedge accounting application for fair value and cash flow hedges, effectiveness assessment, discontinuation, and reference to note 40 for further details.

nodes.title: Financial Liabilities De-recognition and Derivative Hedge Accounting Policies
key_items: Derivative financial instruments and hedge accounting
nodes.summary: The page covers accounting policies for financial liabilities and derivative instruments. It explains that financial liabilities are de-recognised when obligations are discharged, cancelled, or expire, and that differences between proceeds and settlement are recognised over the borrowing term using the effective interest method. For derivatives, the Group uses forwards, swaps, and collars to hedge foreign exchange, base metal price, and interest rate risks. Derivatives are initially and subsequently measured at fair value, with hedge accounting applied where possible, including formal documentation, effectiveness assessment at inception and ongoing, and immediate recognition of ineffective portions in profit and loss.

nodes.title: When hedge accounting is applied:

Additionally, it details employee benefits: defined contribution plans (expense recognition) and defined benefit plans (Projected Unit Credit Method, actuarial valuation, remeasurement in OCI, service cost, past service cost, and balance sheet obligation). Compensated absences are measured at present value using actuarial valuation, with actuarial gains/losses in profit or loss. Inventories are recorded at lower of cost or net realisable value, with cost on weighted average basis, and provisions for slow-moving/obsolete items. Provisions are recognized for present obligations, measured at best estimate, discounted if material, including constructive obligations.

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Employee Benefits, Inventories, and Provisions

nodes.title: Provisions

nodes.title: Accounting Policies: Onerous Contracts and Government Grants

It also covers government grants, recognized at fair value when reasonable assurance exists of receipt and compliance with conditions; grants related to property, plant and equipment are credited to profit or loss over useful lives or another systematic basis reflecting fulfillment of obligations, with uncredited amounts reported as deferred income in the balance sheet.

nodes.title: Income taxes

nodes.title: Sales tax /VAT
nodes.summary: The text details contingencies and commitments regarding tax disputes. It covers GST demands: the Company provides municipal services in Jamshedpur under a lease deed and has agreements with TSUISL, which charges GST; the Company claims input tax credit (ITC) for this and for healthcare services at Tata Main Hospital. Both ITCs were disputed, leading to a Show Cause Notice dated August 3, 2022, confirmed by Order in Original dated June 23, 2023. The Company appealed to Commissioner (Appeals) Ranchi, pending; amount involved is ₹154.54 crore as of March 31, 2025. It also covers sales tax/VAT demands contested by the Group totaling ₹380.98 crore, including ₹29.74 crore for equity accounted investees. Significant demand details: the Company stock transfers goods from Jamshedpur to depots/branches outside Jharkhand without central sales tax, submitting F-Forms; the Commercial Tax Department demanded central sales tax on the difference between outside-state sales value and F-Form value for assessment years 2012-13, 2014-15, 2015-16, and 2016-17, amounting to ₹79.00 crore as of March 31, 2025.

nodes.title: Other taxes, dues and claims
nodes.summary: The text discusses the ORISED matter, detailing the Orissa Rural Infrastructure and Socio-Economic Development Act, 2004, which levied tax on mineral-bearing land. The Company received demands of ₹129 crore for FY05 and FY06, challenged the Act's constitutionality in the Orissa High Court, which ruled in December 2005 that the State lacked legislative authority. The State appealed to the Supreme Court, where the matter was referred to a Constitution Bench. On July 25, 2024, the Supreme Court ruled that the Mines and Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act does not deprive States of the power to tax mineral rights, and directed pending matters to a Regular Bench. An August 14, 2024 order clarified the judgment. The State's appeal remains pending before the Regular Bench.

It also reports other contingent liabilities totaling ₹5,307.12 crore, including ₹113.77 crore for equity-accounted investees. Significant demand (i) concerns a ₹411.08 crore royalty demand by the Deputy Director of Mines, Joda, on iron ore fines; the Company filed a revision petition in 2013, obtained stays, challenged a High Court judgment in 2016, and the Mines Tribunal awaits the Supreme Court's outcome.

An assessment order confirmed royalty on calibrated lump ore and fines from April 2022, with a likely demand of ₹2,696.58 crore as of March 31, 2025. Demand notices totaling ₹3,827.29 crore for excess production from 2000-01 to 2009-10 were issued under MMDR Act, later remanded. Following a Supreme Court judgment, new notices amounting to ₹3,873.35 crore were issued, with the company paying ₹614.41 crore and ₹56.97 crore under protest, and challenging ₹132.91 crore. The Mines Tribunal disposed of revision applications, remanding them to the State Government for fresh hearings.

In Jharkhand, demand notices of ₹2,140.30 crore were challenged; the Revisional Authority set aside the demands, leading the Company to reverse a provision of ₹1,412.89 crore, and the balance of ₹727.41 crore is no longer considered contingent.
